newsitem.title: UK: U.S. jobs data gives mild boost to European bonds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobs data gives mild boost to European bonds.

text.p: U.S. labour data on Friday gave a small boost to European bonds over Treasuries, but investors should be wary on Europe while single currency worries persist, analysts said.

"While the European markets usually move with the U.S. to an extent, they are probably insulated because there is so much uncertainty in the market," said Juli Collins-Thomson, economist at Yamaichi International Europe in London.
At 1319 GMT the 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread was quoted at 94 basis points from 90 after the U.S. unemployment rate fell to 4.8 percent in May -- its lowest since October 1973.
European bonds initially spiked higher on a softer-than expected rise in non-farm payrolls at 138,000 against forecasts of 219,000. But the rally faltered and prices retreated to flat levels.
Collins-Thomson said while the prospect of a U.S. rate rise provided a sharp focus, sentiment in Europe would be dictated by the convergence toward a single currency.
Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International, said Treasuries were favoured over Europe as investors search for yield pick-up and as Europe undergoes huge structural changes.
"U.S.bonds at the moment are certainly attractive to European investors," he told Reuters Financial Television.
He added the data showed the U.S. Federal Reserve may not raise rates in July.

"Markets generally are not going to punish the Fed if they don't move in July so do have a little leverage on timing," Hannah said. A Reuters poll of economists forecast a rise of 219,000 in employment compared with a rise of 142,000 previously. It represents a marked decrease from expectations of above 300,000 a week ago. The reduced forecast stemmed from lack week's benchmark revisions by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The unemployment rate was expected to rise to 5.0 percent from 4.9 in April. Average hourly earnings are expected to rise 0.4 percent compared with a 0.1 percent fall previously.
A low inflation outlook attract investors to yields above seven percent, while yields were unlikely to fall decisively even if data gave concrete evidence of a slowdown.
Strong payroll could weigh on short end while long end underpinned by tame average earnings report.

The gilt market was the winner in Europe. A 25 basis point increase in UK interest rates on Friday removed the uncertainty of a likely near term rate rise and dealers said the move was viewed as positive since it helps to squeeze any future inflation out of the British economy.
By 1400 GMT, the September gilt future contract on LIFFE stood 13 basis points up at 113-26.
Other European bond contracts were scouring a narrow range.

Bund futures stood lower with the September contract losing one basis point on the day to 100.50 while the BTP rallied to a session high of 130.75, then settled back at 130.56, up four basis points from Thursday.
